blocks.text: When a danfo brakes hard, every standing passenger lurches forward. Nothing pushed them — that is exactly the point. Their bodies were already moving at 40 km/h and nothing had yet acted to stop them. Newton put that stubbornness into three laws that between them explain almost every everyday motion.

blocks.markdown:
### The three laws

**First law (law of inertia):** a body continues at rest, or moves with uniform velocity in a straight line, unless acted upon by a **resultant** external force.

**Second law:** the rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the resultant force applied and takes place in the direction of that force. For constant mass this simplifies to $F = ma$.

**Third law:** to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. The two forces act on **different bodies**.

blocks.title: Inertia
blocks.text: The reluctance of a body to change its state of rest or of uniform motion. Mass is the measure of inertia — a loaded lorry is much harder to start and much harder to stop than an empty one, because it has more mass and therefore more inertia.

blocks.caption: Newton's second law: resultant force equals mass times acceleration

blocks.title: Finding the driving force on a car
blocks.prompt: A car of mass 1500 kg accelerates uniformly at 2.0 m/s². The total resistance to motion is 500 N. Calculate the driving force produced by the engine.

steps.text: Newton's second law uses the RESULTANT force, so first find the resultant needed.
The resultant is the driving force minus the resistance.
Add the resistance to both sides.
State the answer with its unit.

blocks.markdown:
### Momentum and impulse

**Momentum** is the product of mass and velocity, $p = mv$, measured in $\text{kg}\,\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-1}$. It is a vector, so direction and sign matter.

**Impulse** is force multiplied by the time for which it acts, $Ft$, measured in $\text{N}\,\text{s}$. From the second law,

$$Ft = mv - mu$$

so impulse equals the change in momentum. Note that $1\ \text{N}\,\text{s}$ and $1\ \text{kg}\,\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-1}$ are the same unit.

blocks.title: Why crash helmets and airbags work
blocks.text: The change in momentum in a crash is fixed by how fast you were going. Since Ft = change in momentum, lengthening the collision time t must reduce the force F. Padding, crumple zones and airbags all buy extra milliseconds and so cut the force on the body.

blocks.markdown:
### Conservation of linear momentum

When no external force acts on a system, its total momentum stays constant:

$$m_1u_1 + m_2u_2 = m_1v_1 + m_2v_2$$

In a **perfectly inelastic** collision the bodies stick together and move off with a common velocity $v$, so the right-hand side becomes $(m_1 + m_2)v$. Kinetic energy is not conserved in such a collision, but momentum always is.

blocks.title: An inelastic collision
blocks.prompt: A trolley of mass 3.0 kg moving at 4.0 m/s collides with a stationary trolley of mass 1.0 kg. The two stick together. Calculate their common velocity after the collision.

steps.text: Write the conservation of momentum equation for the two bodies.
Substitute the values; the second trolley is stationary so u₂ = 0.
Evaluate the left-hand side: the total momentum before the collision.
Divide both sides by the total mass.
State the answer with its unit and direction.

blocks.answer: 3.0 m/s in the original direction of the moving trolley

rows: Foot pushes backwards on the ground
Ground pushes forwards on the foot
Book presses down on the table
Table pushes up on the book
blocks.caption: Action-reaction pairs. Notice that the two forces in each pair always act on different bodies.

blocks.title: The commonest third-law mistake
blocks.text: The weight of a book and the upward push of the table are NOT an action-reaction pair, because both act on the same body — the book. They happen to be equal here only because the book is in equilibrium. The true partner of the book's weight is the equal upward pull the book exerts on the Earth.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: In every momentum problem, choose a positive direction and write it down before substituting. Bodies moving the other way then take negative velocities automatically, and the sign of your answer tells you the final direction. Most lost marks on collision questions are sign errors, not arithmetic.

points: First law: a body keeps its state of rest or uniform motion unless a resultant external force acts; mass measures this inertia.
Second law: resultant force equals rate of change of momentum, which for constant mass gives F = ma.
Third law: action and reaction are equal, opposite, and act on two different bodies.
Momentum p = mv in kg m s⁻¹; impulse Ft equals the change in momentum and is measured in N s.
Total momentum is conserved in any collision or explosion when no external force acts, even when kinetic energy is not.
